title: Throughput Garden: weekly briefing — kernel / KV / batching
content:
Summary:
This week's standup covered three focus areas: kernel handshake adjustments for cold starts, a small-window experiment to reduce KV cache shadowing, and an updated backpressure heuristic for the batching coordinator. Overall signal: steady improvement on p95 for short sequences (<=64 tokens), lingering tail spikes for p99 on mixed-length traffic.

Attendees:
- Priya (owner)
- Ethan (benchmarks / perf tools)
- Marta (kernel / CUDA ops)
- Omar (batching coordinator)
- Tania (SRE - telemetry)

Top-line numbers (compare to last Wed):
- p50 latency (<=64 tokens): 24ms -> 22ms (improved)
- p95 latency (<=64 tokens): 48ms -> 39ms (improved with kernel handshake fix)
- p99 latency (mixed): 420ms -> 380ms (still noisy)
- Throughput (tokens/s per T4-equivalent pod): 1.9k -> 2.05k (microbatching tuned)
- KV cache hit rate (prefix windows <=128): 73% -> 78% (after shadow-window shrink)

What we changed this week:
1) Kernel handshake timeout reduction (Marta / PR #1847)
   - Problem: cold kernel handshakes were adding ~8–12ms at the start of many short requests when the runtime negotiated tiling affinity and chosen kernel set.
   - Change: reduced handshake timeouts and opportunistically reuse previous kernel selection metadata for the same model family if device topology unchanged.
   - Result: immediate p95 improvement on short requests and fewer short-lived kernel fallback paths observed in logs.

2) KV shadow window shrink (Ethan / INF-2339)
   - Problem: long shadow windows caused stale KV prefix entries to block cache eviction during bursts, reducing effective hit rate under spike.
   - Experiment: reduced shadow retention on the shadow cache from 1.2s to 350ms for sequences <=128 tokens; added a decay-weight to mark entries as "cold" sooner when capacity pressure is detected.
   - Result: hit rate rose from 73% -> 78% in synthetic spike tests; however, p99 still shows transient spikes during the exact ramp-up window.

3) Batching backpressure heuristic tweak (Omar)
   - Problem: batching coordinator allowed a few inflight microbatches to grow too large under tail-heavy workloads, causing head-of-line blocking on small latency-sensitive requests.
   - Change: introduced a soft cap on microbatch size for routes tagged "latency-sensitive" and a fast-path to preempt an in-progress microbatch if sufficient low-latency tokens queue up.
   - Result: small-request p95 improved, but throughput drops slightly (~3%) for non-latency-tagged routes. We think this is acceptable tradeoff for targeted routes.

Open experiments and notes:
- Hybrid kernel selection policy: Marta is prototyping a quick-check cache for kernel sets keyed by (model-version, device-layout, max_seq). Early numbers show fewer kernel fallbacks but a small memory overhead (2–3MB per worker). Need to evaluate at scale.
- Aggressive KV compaction: idea to compact prefix entries by canonicalizing repeated token spans. Conceptual; requires more profiling to ensure no decode regressions.
- Microbatch preemption correctness: Omar to add formalized invariant tests (race conditions around redispatch). Put on CI with stress harness.

Telemetry and debugging
- New trace tag added: runtime.kernel.handshake_path which records selection path and fallbacks for postmortem. Instrumented in staging as of Tuesday.
- Aggregated logs show one host (us-west-2-a) with elevated kernel fallback rates; SRE is isolating node-level scheduler noise.

Action items (owners and due dates):
- Marta: land quick-check kernel cache prototype into bench harness, smoke test on perf cluster by 2028-06-16. (blocking: memory estimate validation)
- Ethan: run end-to-end spike test with shadow-window shrink across 50 cluster replicas and report p99 waterfall by 2028-06-15.
- Omar: implement preemption invariants and add stress CI job, target 2028-06-20.
- Tania (SRE): quarantine the anomalous us-west-2-a hosts and collect scheduler traces; update on 2028-06-13.
- Priya: draft rollout plan for batching soft cap across latency-tagged routes; share in #runtime-sync by 2028-06-14.

Risks / things to watch
- Memory overhead of kernel quick-check cache at scale; worst-case could push pod memory by a few percent. If pressure observed, we will fallback to LRU with size cap.
- Eager shadow-window shrink might increase cold-miss CPU overhead for very bursty long-sequence workloads. Monitor token-processing CPU profile.
- Preemption adds complexity to correctness surface; risk of duplicate token emission if race not covered. CI stress tests must be thorough before canary.

Notes from retro briefly:
- What worked: Pairing kernel devs with benchmarks team produced fast feedback loops; landed handshake tweak within 48 hours.
- What didn't: We under-indexed SRE input on host scheduler fuzziness (us-west-2-a). Need earlier SRE presence in kernel rollouts.
- Improvement: Add a rollout checklist item: "confirm scheduler variance < X ms across cluster" before kernel metadata caching is enabled.

Questions to discuss in next sync:
- What should the default microbatch soft cap be for default routes? (0.75x of historical median?)
- Do we conservatively enable shadow-window shrink only for models with stable prefix distributions?
- Is there appetite to push kernel selection metadata into a small shared in-node cache (vs per-worker) to save memory?

Quick links and artifacts: GH PR: redwood/serving-runtime#1847 (kernel handshake), JIRA INF-2339 (kv-shadow shrink experiment), perf dashboard: https://perf.redwood.ai/dash/serving-runtime/throughput-garden (staging view).

Loose TODOs / brain dump:
- Try microbatch size histogram per route (not just global) — helps tuning soft caps per product.
- Investigate canonicalization idea only on prefix shapes that show >3x duplication.
- Add a "latency-sensitive" flag to our model catalog to avoid manual route tagging for common product families.

End of brief.

(Internal: keep this doc as a rolling weekly note for the "throughput garden" initiative; will snapshot and attach to the sprint board at the end of the week.)
